related_questions.question: How does breast cancer affect a person's body?
related_questions.snippet: Breast cancer can affect the body in various ways, including physical and emotional changes. It can cause tiredness, swelling, and changes to the skin and hair. It can also affect other parts of the body. Breast cancer is a serious disease in which abnormal breast cells divide and grow uncontrollably.

related_questions.question: What happens if breast cancer is not treated?
related_questions.snippet: If left untreated, breast cancer may spread from breast tissue to other parts of the body, such as the bones, liver or lungs. Breast cancer affects both males and females, although it is much less common in males. There are some pre-cancerous breast conditions, also referred to as 'pre-invasive' or 'carcinoma in situ'.

related_questions.question: How long can someone live with breast cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: The length of time someone can live with breast cancer varies significantly based on several factors, primarily the stage of the cancer at diagnosis. For early-stage breast cancer (Stages 0-II), the five-year survival rate is very high, often close to 100%. However, for advanced or metastatic (Stage IV) breast cancer, the prognosis is more complex, with some individuals living only a few months, while others may live for 10 years or more.
snippet_highlighted_words: For early-stage breast cancer (Stages 0-II), the five-year survival rate is very high, often close to 100%

list.title: Early-stage (Stages 0-II):
list.snippet: Five-year survival rates are generally very high, often above 90%. For example, Stage 0 and I breast cancer have a survival rate close to 100%.

list.title: Stage III:
list.snippet: Around 72% of women with Stage III breast cancer survive five years, according to the Arizona Center for Cancer Care.

list.title: Stage IV (Metastatic):
list.snippet: The five-year survival rate for Stage IV breast cancer is significantly lower, with about 22% of women surviving five years, according to the Arizona Center for Cancer Care. However, some women with Stage IV breast cancer can live for many years with treatment.
Stage of cancer: This is the most significant factor influencing survival.
Cancer type and subtype: Different types of breast cancer (e.g., HER2-positive, triple-negative) have different prognoses.
Individual health and response to treatment: Age, overall health, and how well a person responds to treatment can all impact survival.
Hormone receptor status: If the cancer is hormone receptor-positive (estrogen and/or progesterone receptor positive), it may respond well to hormone therapy, which can improve survival.
HER2 status: If the cancer is HER2-positive, targeted therapies may be effective, impacting survival.
Grade of the tumor: Higher-grade tumors (more aggressive) may have a poorer prognosis.

list.title: Survival rates are based on averages:
list.snippet: These numbers are based on statistical data from large groups of people and may not accurately reflect an individual's specific situation.

list.title: Treatment advances:
list.snippet: Medical advancements have improved survival rates for many types of breast cancer, especially metastatic breast cancer, over time.

list.title: Quality of life:
list.snippet: Treatment for breast cancer, especially advanced stages, can impact quality of life. It's important to discuss the potential side effects and long-term consequences of treatment with your healthcare team.

list.title: Individualized approach:
list.snippet: Prognosis is highly individualized. A doctor who knows your specific case can provide a more accurate prognosis and treatment plan.

text_blocks.snippet: Breast cancer is a disease where malignant (cancerous) cells form in the breast tissue. It typically begins in the milk ducts or lobules and can spread to other parts of the body if not treated. While it's most common in women, men can also be affected.
snippet_highlighted_words: a disease where malignant (cancerous) cells form in the breast tissue

list.snippet: Breast cancer develops when cells in the breast start to grow and divide uncontrollably.
These abnormal cells can form a tumor, which may or may not be cancerous.
Cancerous tumors are malignant, meaning they can invade surrounding tissues and potentially spread to other parts of the body (metastasis).
The most common types of breast cancer include invasive ductal carcinoma (starting in the milk ducts) and invasive lobular carcinoma (starting in the milk-producing glands).
The breast is made up of lobules (milk-producing glands), ducts (tubes that carry milk to the nipple), and connective tissue.
Most breast cancers begin in the ducts or lobules.
Breast cancer can spread through blood vessels and lymph vessels.
When it spreads to other parts of the body, it is called metastatic breast cancer or secondary breast cancer.
This spread can be to nearby lymph nodes, or to distant areas like the bones, liver, or lungs.
Breast cancer is most common in women, but men can also develop it.
It's the second most common cancer in women in the United States.
Early detection through screening (like mammograms) is crucial for successful treatment and better outcomes.
Screening can help find breast cancer before symptoms appear, when it's often smaller and less likely to have spread.
